newsitem.title: EGYPT: BMW to open assembly plant in Egypt.
newsitem.headline: BMW to open assembly plant in Egypt.

text.p: German car maker BMW is opening its first assembly plant in the Middle East in the second quarter of 1997 to expand its market share, officials said.

Horst Teltschik, Bayerische Motoren-Werke board member who oversees emerging markets, said BMW will open the plant in Egypt by May partly because it was hopeful of Middle East stability and saw benefits from investing as the country privatises.
"BMW is announcing that we will start an assembly plant next year close to Cairo...to develop the Egyptian market," he told Reuters in an interview late on Monday.
BMW sold 263 cars in Egypt in 1995 and this year expects sales of 4,000 BMWs in the Middle East, a statement said.

"Our share just now is not very high. We will hopefully see this year 400 units," Teltschik said. "But our experience is when we are entering a market like Egypt by assembling the cars, the sales will raise immediately. This is our hope for Egypt.
"The Middle East is an important market for us, it's a growing market...Because of the peace process we do hope that the region will be more stabilised than it was in the past."
He said the plant would assemble medium-sized, five series BMWs. It will have an initial capacity of 2,500 cars per year.
Other car makers in Egypt include Nissan, General Motors, Citroen, Hyundai and Suzuki. Mercedes is setting up a plant.

"The fact that companies like BMW are coming to Egypt is a ...signal, because it says something about our confidence in the political stability and economic development," Teltschik said. "We are optimistic that the market will grow, and we are interested to participate in that market from the beginning.
"If there might be a chance to enter other markets from Egypt we will do it," he said.
The BMW statement said in two years a quarter of BMW investments in the Middle East would focus on Egypt. It has plans for import centres in Jeddah, Syria and Palestinian areas.
The BMWs will be assembled with an Egyptian partner from completely knocked down (CKD) kits with 40 percent local value added, BMW sales director Luder Paysen told a news conference.
This means BMW can import car parts at reduced tariff rates. "We always decide on a CKD investment when high tariff barriers make imports of cars from Germany difficult," he said.
Paysen said the market could reach 100,000 in four years. If BMW can "capture five percent...we can be satisfied," he said.
